title: Rahula awakens
hookLine: the Buddha teaches the six senses as not-self, and Rahula awakens

lines: THE BOY WITH THE MIRROR, GROWN.
UNDER A TREE IN THE DARK FOREST.
cards: A boy taught with a mirror, then a young monk told to be like the earth and like water: Rahula has come up before in this collection. Now, in the hundred and forty-seventh discourse, he's grown.

One day near Savatthi, the Buddha reflects that the qualities that ripen into freedom have ripened in Rahula. So after the alms round he says: Rahula, bring your sitting cloth. We'll spend the day in the Dark Forest.
A father and a son walk out of the city and sit down under a tree. The text adds that many thousands of gods followed them, wanting to hear.

teach.b: The teaching is a string of questions, and Rahula answers every one himself. Rahula, is the eye permanent or impermanent? Impermanent, venerable sir.
And what is impermanent, is it suffering or ease? Suffering. And what is impermanent, suffering, bound to change: is it fit to be seen as, this is mine, this I am, this is my self?
No, venerable sir. Then the same three questions for forms, the things the eye sees. For eye-consciousness, the seeing itself.

For eye-contact, the meeting of eye and form. For the feeling, perception, choices and awareness that come out of that meeting. Then all of it again, for the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body and the mind.
The Buddha doesn't announce a doctrine and ask Rahula to accept it. He asks, and lets his son look and say what he sees. The Pali word under every answer is anicca: impermanent, changing.
Not only the world out there, but the instrument doing the looking, and the looking itself.
Seeing this, the Buddha says, a noble disciple grows disenchanted with the eye, with forms, with seeing, and becomes dispassionate, and through dispassion the mind is freed.
While he was speaking, the text says, Rahula's mind was freed from the taints, through not clinging.
And the gods who had followed saw something too: whatever has the nature to arise, all of that has the nature to cease.
In the Vinaya's story of his going forth, the boy Rahula asks his father for his inheritance. Here, under a tree, he receives it, as questions.

how: Theravada teachers use this discourse's three questions as a pattern for insight practice: is it permanent, is it unsatisfactory, is it fit to be called self?

o: Rahula's first day as a novice monk
Rahula waking from a long night's sleep
Rahula freed, seeing that even the senses change

p: where father and son spent the day
the meeting of eye and form

s: the Buddha gives Rahula a long lecture and Rahula listens in silence
it's a string of questions, and Rahula answers every one himself.
the questions cover not just the eye but the seeing and the contact too
forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact and what arises from it, then all six senses.
the text says many gods followed them to the forest
and while Rahula was freed, they saw that whatever arises has the nature to cease.

games.q: you're Rahula, under the tree. the Buddha asks: what is impermanent and bound to change, is it fit to be seen as 'this is my self'? what do you say?
o: yes, if it's my own eye.
only the mind is my self.
games.why: Rahula answers no, every time, for every sense. the Buddha lets him see it for himself instead of telling him.

practice: Eyes open for a moment, notice something you're seeing, and the seeing itself shifting: light, focus, a blink. Then close your eyes: a sound arrives and fades, the chair under you, air on your hands, changing even while you notice.
Each time something arises, say quietly, changing, not as a sad word, just as a true one.

wordCard.voice: Rahula awakens. Anicca, impermanence, seen in the senses themselves: the eye, what it sees, and the seeing. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali anicca: impermanent, changing. Sanskrit anitya. here, the eye, what it sees, and the seeing itself.

carryVoice: Your line: all of it changing. Said plainly, it can be a calm word, not a sad one. Until tomorrow.
